statement: In 14 adults with alcohol use disorder who had recently completed detoxification (one open-label feasibility study in the UK, all White British, with no comparison group), an eight-week course of ten psychotherapy sessions that included two MDMA sessions was followed, 3 months after treatment, by self-reported drinking at least two WHO risk levels lower than at baseline in 9 of the 14 (64%; 95% CI 35% to 87%), which the authors' Bayesian analysis restates as a success rate of 55% to 63%; self-reported craving, a four-item sleep score and self-compassion also improved in the 13 or 14 with data, while quality of life did not change significantly after correction (11 with data). The trial registry places the drinking baseline before detoxification, the outcomes were self-reported by people who knew they had taken MDMA, the two-level endpoint was not a registered outcome, and the registered 6- and 9-month results are not in this report, so none of these changes can be attributed to MDMA. No randomized or otherwise controlled trial of MDMA-assisted therapy in alcohol use disorder was among the sources read. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small UK study, 14 adults with alcohol use disorder who had just been through detox had a talking-therapy course with two MDMA sessions. Three months later, 9 of the 14 reported drinking much less than at the start (which seems to mean before detox). There was no group without MDMA, and drinking was self-reported, so we cannot tell whether MDMA helped.
population: Adults aged 18 to 65 (registry) with a primary DSM-5 diagnosis of alcohol use disorder who had completed detoxification; excluded: psychotic, bipolar I or personality disorders, serious suicide risk, cardiovascular or severe liver disease, regular ecstasy use, other drug dependence, and antidepressants unless stopped
exposure: An eight-week recovery-based psychotherapy course of ten sessions, two of them with MDMA, with an overnight stay after each MDMA session
comparator: None: each participant's own baseline (for drinking, apparently drinking before detoxification, per the registry)
outcome: Reduction of at least two WHO drinking risk levels (Timeline Followback) 3 months after treatment; craving (PACS, OCDS), sleep, quality of life (SF-36), self-compassion and empathy at 3 months
magnitude: Two-level WHO risk reduction: 9 of 14 (proportion .64; binomial test against 50%, P = .423; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87); mean posterior success rate 0.63 (credible interval 0.40 to 0.85) with a flat prior and 0.55 (0.33 to 0.77) with a Beta(1,3) prior (editors' check: posterior means 0.625 and 0.556). Three months vs baseline: PACS −5.50 (95% CI 0.5 to 13; n = 13); OCDS obsessive −5.00 (2.00 to 8.50) and compulsive −5.00 (1.00 to 9.00); four-item sleep score −2.00 (n = 14); Self-Compassion Scale +12.1 (9.09 to 14.4; n = 13); no SF-36 subscale significant after Bonferroni correction (n = 11). Within-group changes only.

evidence.locator: Results › Bayesian analysis of World Health Organization drinking risk level at 3 months follow-up, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
evidence.extracted: 9 of 14 reached a two-level reduction in WHO drinking risk at 3 months; binomial test against 50%: proportion .64, P = .423, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87; mean posterior 0.63 (credible interval 0.40 to 0.85) with a flat prior and 0.55 (0.33 to 0.77) with the sceptical Beta(1,3) prior.

evidence.locator: Results › Drinking behavior at 3 months follow-up, 1st paragraph; Fig. 2 legend
evidence.extracted: At 3 months vs baseline (n = 13): PACS total difference 5.50 (95% CI .5 to 13), P = .031; OCDS obsessive 5.00 (2.00 to 8.50), P = .006; OCDS compulsive 5.00 (1.00 to 9.00), P = .021; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

evidence.locator: Results › Quality of life, sleep, well-being, and psychosocial functioning measures › Quality of life, Sleep and Self-compassion, 1st paragraphs; Fig. 3 legend
evidence.extracted: SF-36 (n = 11): no subscale significant after Bonferroni correction; four PSQI-derived sleep items (n = 14): difference 2.00, P = .041; Self-Compassion Scale (n = 13): +12.1 (95% CI 9.09 to 14.4), P < .001.

Fourteen participants with alcohol use disorder who had recently undergone detoxification completed the eight-week course of ten sessions, two with MDMA; 8 men and 6 women, mean age 48, all White British.

evidence.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04158778 (API v2) › Status; Outcome Measures
evidence.extracted: Single-group open-label phase 1 study, actual start 18 April 2018, first submitted 31 January 2019 (retrospective registration); drinking registered as change by Timeline Followback from pre-detoxification (screening) levels to session 10 and 3, 6 and 9 months; no two-level WHO endpoint registered; questionnaires registered at 3, 6 and 9 months; no results posted.

The authors call the study an open-label trial with a small population, acknowledge possible Type I error inflation, call the findings hypothesis-generating rather than evidence of efficacy, and ask for randomized placebo-controlled trials that measure de-blinding and expectancy, and for long-term follow-up.

The authors compare the 55% to 63% success rate with 68% of patients reaching a two-level WHO risk reduction at the end of treatment in secondary analyses of the COMBINE study and Project MATCH: a comparison across studies, not within this one.

risk_of_bias.note: Critical: no comparison group, pre-detoxification baseline, unblinded self-report, unregistered endpoint.

grade.reasoning: One single-arm open-label study of 14 people; for the question of effect it is non-randomized, so it starts low. Risk of bias two levels (ROBINS-I critical): no comparison group; a drinking baseline that the registry places before detoxification, so a fall after detoxification is expected whatever the treatment; self-reported outcomes from people who knew they had taken MDMA; unexplained missing questionnaire data; an unregistered endpoint, with the registered 6- and 9-month results unreported. Imprecision one level: 14 people, with a 95% interval from 35% to 87% for the endpoint. Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to this population and time point; publication bias not assessable from one study. The relation is 'insufficient evidence': the design cannot show whether MDMA-assisted therapy changes drinking, and the statement only describes what was observed.

verification.flag_note: The original report of the same 14 participants (Sessa et al., 2021, J Psychopharmacol, doi 10.1177/0269881121991792) is not free and was not read; its safety and 9-month drinking data should be added before this claim is shown.

statement: In adults with moderate to severe anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, almost all with cancer (one randomized pilot trial at a single California clinic: 13 on MDMA, 5 on an inactive placebo), two MDMA sessions within manualized psychotherapy, compared with placebo with the same psychotherapy, were followed one month later by a larger fall in self-reported trait anxiety (STAI-Trait, scale 20 to 80: −23.5 vs −8.8 points; difference 14.7, 95% CI −0.5 to 29.9, editors' calculation; P = 0.056). The difference was not statistically significant and its interval runs from no difference to a very large one; the MDMA group started 5 points more anxious, and participants guessed their allocation correctly in 31 of 36 sessions. After the placebo group crossed over to MDMA, scores stayed lower at 6 and 12 months, with no control group left. The evidence is insufficient to say whether MDMA-assisted therapy reduces anxiety in people with a life-threatening illness. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small trial, 18 adults with anxiety linked to cancer or another serious illness had talking therapy with either MDMA or a dummy pill. A month later, anxiety had dropped more in the MDMA group, but the difference could be chance, and most people could tell which pill they had.
population: Adults with a life-threatening cancer or non-dementing neurological illness (17 of 18 with neoplasms), life expectancy of at least 9 months, STAI-Trait of 45 or more and anxiety mainly related to the illness, off psychiatric medicines; excluded: ongoing first-line treatment such as initial chemotherapy, cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease, brain tumours, diabetes, psychotic and bipolar I disorders
exposure: MDMA in two blinded day-long sessions 2 to 4 weeks apart within manualized non-directive psychotherapy (three preparatory sessions and integration sessions after each)
comparator: Inactive placebo (lactose) with the same psychotherapy
outcome: Change in STAI-Trait from baseline to one month after the second session (primary); secondary anxiety, depression, sleep and well-being measures; uncontrolled follow-up to 12 months after crossover
magnitude: STAI-Trait change −23.5 (SD 13.2; n = 13) vs −8.8 (14.7; n = 5), P = 0.0558; Hedges' g 1.03, printed with a 95% CI of −5.25 to 7.31 that cannot be right (editors' approximate interval −0.05 to 2.12); raw difference 14.7 points, 95% CI −0.5 to 29.9 (editors' calculation, pooled t(16) = 2.06). Of 20 uncorrected secondary comparisons, only posttraumatic growth and mindfulness reached P = 0.04. After crossover, uncontrolled (n = 17): STAI-Trait 61.1 at baseline, 33.6 at 6 months and 34.2 at 12 months.

evidence.extracted: STAI-Trait change from baseline to one month after the second blinded session: −23.5 (SD 13.2) on MDMA vs −8.8 (14.7) on placebo, P = 0.0558; endpoint 38.9 vs 48.6; Hedges' g 1.03 printed with a 95% CI of −5.25 to 7.31. Editors' calculation: difference 14.7 points, 95% CI −0.5 to 29.9; approximate CI for g −0.05 to 2.12.
Placebo change scores ranged from −1 to −35 (median −3); excluding the one placebo participant with −35, a post hoc comparison gave P = 0.0066; the prespecified comparison gave P = 0.0558.
Baseline STAI-Trait 62.5 (7.3) on MDMA vs 57.4 (5.2) on placebo; history of PTSD 11 of 13 (84.6%) vs 2 of 5 (40.0%); the primary analysis compared unadjusted change scores.
At the end of each blinded session participants guessed their allocation correctly in 31 of 36 sessions (86.1%) and the co-therapists in 32 of 36 (88.9%).

Secondary outcomes at the primary endpoint: posttraumatic growth (P = 0.04) and mindfulness (P = 0.04) favoured MDMA; STAI-State (P = 0.10), BDI-II (P = 0.36), PSQI (P = 0.05), MADRS (P = 0.41), GAF (P = 0.52) and self-compassion (P = 0.21) did not differ significantly; no correction for about 20 tests.

After both groups had received three MDMA sessions (n = 17, no control group): STAI-Trait 61.1 (7.0) at baseline, 36.4 (9.5) at treatment exit, 33.6 (8.3) at 6 months and 34.2 (10.3) at 12 months; F(3,48) = 51.39.

evidence.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02427568 (API v2) › Status; Outcome Measures; Results › Outcome Measures
evidence.extracted: First submitted 13 April 2015, before the start on 14 May 2015; registered primary outcome change in STAI-Trait to one month after the second session; posted results give the same changes (−23.5 [13.2] and −8.8 [14.7]) for 13 and 5 participants.

risk_of_bias.note: Participant-reported outcome with allocation evident; baseline imbalance with unadjusted analysis.

imprecision.note: Five controls; interval includes no difference.

grade.reasoning: One randomized trial: starts high. Risk of bias two levels (very serious, RoB 2 high for the measurement of the outcome): the primary outcome is self-reported while participants identified their allocation in 86% of sessions and expectancy was not measured; the MDMA group also started with higher anxiety and change scores were not adjusted for baseline, which could favour MDMA through regression to the mean. Imprecision two levels: 18 participants with only 5 controls, and the 95% interval of the difference runs from about −0.5 to 30 points. Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to the trial population and endpoint. The relation is 'insufficient evidence' because neither an effect nor its absence is shown with precision.

statement: In autistic adults with marked to very severe social anxiety (one randomized pilot trial at a single California site: 8 randomized to MDMA and 4 to an inactive placebo, of whom 7 and 4 were analysed), two MDMA sessions within psychotherapy, compared with placebo with the same psychotherapy, were followed one month later by a larger fall in interview-rated social anxiety (Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale: −44.1 vs −19.3 points; difference 24.8, 95% CI 1.9 to 47.9; P = 0.037), and the difference was similar at 6 months (P = 0.036). Participants identified their allocation in 22 of 23 sessions, two dose groups were pooled (in the registry the lower-dose group improved more), and the interval runs from a trivial to a very large difference, so the evidence is insufficient to say how much, if at all, MDMA reduces social anxiety in autistic adults. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small trial, 12 autistic adults with strong social anxiety had talking therapy with MDMA or a dummy pill. Social anxiety dropped more with MDMA, but almost everyone could tell which pill they had, and the trial was too small to show how big any benefit is.
population: Autistic adults aged 21 or older (ADOS-2 Module 4) with an LSAS of 60 or more, MDMA-naive by self-report, physically healthy and psychologically stable
exposure: MDMA in two blinded 8-hour sessions about a month apart (two dose subgroups, pooled), with three preparatory sessions including mindfulness skills and three integrative sessions after each
comparator: Inactive placebo (lactose) with the same psychotherapy
outcome: Change in Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale total from baseline to one month after the second session (primary) and to 6 months
magnitude: LSAS change −44.1 (SD 14.8; n = 7) vs −19.3 (18.8; n = 4); t(9) = 2.451, P = 0.037; 95% CI of the difference 1.92 to 47.87 (editors' recalculation 1.8 to 47.8); placebo-subtracted d 1.4, printed CI −0.074 to 2.874 (editors' approximation 0.04 to 2.76). Six months: −47.7 (14.7) vs −23.3 (18.0), P = 0.036. Fall of 20 points or more: 6 of 7 vs 2 of 4. Registry results by dose group: lower-dose group −51.0, higher-dose group −39.0, placebo −19.3.

evidence.extracted: LSAS: placebo 83.3 (11.9) at baseline and 64.0 (13.3) at the primary endpoint, change −19.3 (18.8); MDMA 91.8 (15.8) and 46.4 (15.2), change −44.1 (14.8); t(9) = 2.451, P = 0.037, CI 1.92 to 47.87; placebo-subtracted d 1.4 (CI −0.074 to 2.874); MDMA n = 7 after baseline.

evidence.locator: Results › Clinical response, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3
evidence.extracted: Six months: placebo change −23.3 (18.0), MDMA −47.7 (14.7); t(9) = 2.454, P = 0.036; within the MDMA group, primary endpoint to 6 months P = 0.307; a fall of 20 points or more in 6 of 7 on MDMA vs 2 of 4 on placebo (Table 3; the text gives 6 of 8).

Participants guessed their treatment wrongly in one of 8 placebo sessions and in none of the 15 MDMA sessions (correct in 22 of 23); the two therapists were wrong in 2 and 1 of 8 placebo sessions and in 2 of 15 MDMA sessions each.

evidence.locator: Fig. 1 (CONSORT diagram, image); Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Of 8 randomized to MDMA, one was withdrawn after randomization because they had been enrolled with hypertension and a recent substance use disorder within the exclusion window; 7 MDMA and 4 placebo participants were analysed, without imputation; the two dose subgroups were combined.

evidence.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02008396 (API v2) › Status; Results › Outcome Measures
evidence.extracted: Registered 6 December 2013, before the start on 11 April 2014; LSAS change to one month after session 2 posted by group: lower-dose MDMA group −51.0 (8.19), higher-dose group −39.0 (17.57), placebo −19.3 (18.77); posted denominators 4, 4 and 3, while weights of 3 and 4 reproduce the paper's pooled MDMA values (editors' calculation).

The authors call the sample small, too small to compare doses, consider blinding with an inactive placebo adequate because one participant and both investigators made incorrect guesses, and acknowledge that observable MDMA effects might contribute to efficacy.

risk_of_bias.note: Allocation evident in 22 of 23 sessions with a participant-reported interview outcome.

grade.reasoning: One randomized trial: starts high. Risk of bias two levels (very serious, RoB 2 high for the measurement of the outcome): the LSAS interview scores participants' own reports of fear and avoidance, and participants identified their allocation in 22 of 23 sessions, with no measure of expectancy; one MDMA participant was withdrawn after randomization. Imprecision two levels: 11 analysed, and the 95% interval of the difference runs from about 2 to 48 points (the printed interval for d reaches zero). Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to the trial population and endpoints. The relation is 'insufficient evidence' because the trial cannot show the size of any effect with precision; the statement reports the observed difference.

statement: In couples in which one partner had PTSD (two small uncontrolled studies sharing an author: 6 White heterosexual couples in which both partners took MDMA twice within a condensed course of cognitive-behavioral conjoint therapy, and 8 US veteran couples in which only the veteran took MDMA twice within an eight-session brief version), clinician-rated PTSD symptoms fell after treatment (CAPS-5, scale 0 to 80: from about 41 to 19 in the first study, with 5 of 6 patients no longer meeting PTSD criteria; a mean fall of 16 points from 39 in the second, with 3 of 8 no longer meeting criteria and a rebound of about 6 points by 6 months), and both partners' relationship satisfaction rose (in the second study it partly fell back, and one partner's worsened). All couples completed treatment and no serious adverse event was reported. Neither study had a comparison group, the conjoint therapy improves PTSD without MDMA, and in the veteran study loss of diagnosis was about as frequent as with the brief therapy alone in an earlier trial in the same population, so whether MDMA adds anything is not known. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In two small studies, couples in which one partner had PTSD had couples therapy that included MDMA sessions. PTSD and relationship scores improved, and no one had a serious side effect. But neither study had a group without MDMA, and this couples therapy also helps without it, so we do not know if MDMA added anything.
population: Couples (married or committed, almost all heterosexual) in which one partner had chronic PTSD on the CAPS-5 and the other did not; severe relationship aggression or intimate partner violence and current substance use disorders excluded; psychiatric medicines stopped for the PTSD partner (and, in the first study, both partners)
exposure: Two MDMA sessions within cognitive-behavioral conjoint therapy for PTSD: both partners dosed within the full 15-session protocol condensed into 7 weeks (first study), or only the partner with PTSD dosed within an 8-session brief protocol with integration sessions drawing on couple therapy (second study)
comparator: None: change from baseline in each study
outcome: CAPS-5 PTSD severity and diagnosis; relationship satisfaction (Couples Satisfaction Index) and other relational measures; adverse events; up to 6 months
magnitude: First study (6 couples; model-estimated means): CAPS-5 41.42 (SD 5.76) before treatment, 19.37 (13.71) after and 15.52 (15.22) at 6 months (within-group d 2.10 and 2.25); registry: CAPS-5 change −25.7 (SD 13.89); Couples Satisfaction Index, patients 105.37 to 127.00 (d 0.82) and partners 98.10 to 125.34 (d 0.64) after treatment. Second study (8 veteran couples): CAPS-5 39.13 (10.56) at baseline, mean fall 16.1 (SD 11.4) during treatment, response 5 of 8, loss of diagnosis 3 of 8, remission 2 of 8, rebound 6.3 points by 6 months; satisfaction d 1.83 (veterans) and 1.29 (partners) during treatment, rebound d −0.68 and −0.47; reliable improvement in 10 of 16 people and reliable deterioration in 1 partner.

evidence.locator: 2. Results › 2.1 PTSD and patient comorbid outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 2 and 3
evidence.extracted: Six couples: CAPS-5 41.42 (5.76) before treatment, 19.37 (13.71) after, 17.43 (17.14) at 3 months and 15.52 (15.22) at 6 months (estimated means); B = −4.64, P < .001; within-group d 2.10, 1.88 and 2.25; all but one patient had a sustained remission of the clinician-assessed PTSD diagnosis.

evidence.locator: 2. Results › 2.2 Intimate relationship outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 2 and 3
evidence.extracted: Couples Satisfaction Index: patients 105.37 (13.39) to 127.00 after treatment and 130.78 at 6 months, B = 4.55, P < .05, d 0.82 to 1.22; partners 98.10 (50.81) to 125.34 and 130.10, B = 5.73, P < .05, d 0.64 to 0.80; one patient satisfied at baseline was dissatisfied afterwards.
All six couples completed the protocol and there were no serious adverse events; the authors state that the lack of randomization or a control condition severely limits the conclusions.

evidence.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02876172 (API v2) › Results › Outcome Measures; Adverse Events
evidence.extracted: Posted results: CAPS-5 at the primary endpoint 16.3 (13.71), change −25.7 (13.89), n = 6; all 6 patients and all 6 partners had at least one non-serious adverse event up to 2 months after the last MDMA session; no serious events or deaths.

evidence.locator: Results › Outcomes › Trauma-Related Outcomes and Relationship Quality Outcomes, 1st paragraphs; Tables 1 and 2
evidence.extracted: Same six couples: the patient's posttraumatic growth rose as rated by patients (B = 7.30) and partners (B = 7.63), both P < 0.001; perceived support and social intimacy rose for both partners (intimacy B = 4.12 and 3.10); relationship depth did not change; the printed SORTS means duplicate another measure's values (card reporting issue).

evidence.locator: RESULTS › PTSD symptom severity, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3 note
evidence.extracted: Eight veterans: CAPS-5 39.13 (10.56) at baseline; during treatment d = −1.25, mean fall 16.1 points (SD 11.4; range 3 to 34); response 5 of 8, loss of diagnosis 3 of 8, remission 2 of 8; rebound during follow-up of 6.3 points (d = 0.29).

Relationship satisfaction (CSI-32): d = 1.83 for veterans and 1.29 for partners during treatment, mean rise 27.9 (31.8) and 19.8 (23.1); rebound d = −0.68 and −0.47 during follow-up; reliable improvement in 10 of 16, reliable deterioration in 1 partner.

The authors report that CBCT without MDMA has shown large reductions in PTSD symptoms (gs 1.28 to 1.71, citing Monson et al., 2024) and that their eight-session brief CBCT, without MDMA, reduced PTSD in veterans (ds 1.05 to 1.12; Morland et al., 2022) with smaller relationship gains; these figures are second-hand.

Loss of diagnosis (37.5%) and remission (25%) were lower than in the phase 3 MDMA trials and, the authors say, closer to brief CBCT without MDMA in the same population; the open-label design, small sample and lack of a comparison condition preclude causal inference.

evidence.locator: RESULTS › Safety › AEs and Medication management, 1st paragraphs; RESULTS › Feasibility and acceptability
evidence.extracted: All couples completed every session; no serious adverse events; every veteran had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event; one veteran's second MDMA session was rescheduled after a cocaine-positive urine test.

risk_of_bias.note: Critical: no comparison; base therapy effective without MDMA.

grade.reasoning: Two uncontrolled studies (14 couples in all), non-randomized: start low. Risk of bias two levels (ROBINS-I critical in both): no comparison group, and the base therapy is an established treatment that improves PTSD on its own, so MDMA's contribution cannot be separated from the therapy, time or expectation; outcomes unblinded. Imprecision one level: 6 and 8 couples. Inconsistency not rated down: both studies improved, though the second rebounded. Status 'replicated by the same team' because the studies share an author (Anne C. Wagner) and a related protocol; the second sample is independent. The relation is 'insufficient evidence' about any added effect of MDMA.

statement: In 12 adults with moderate to severe major depressive disorder, mostly recurrent (one open-label proof-of-principle study in Norway, with no comparison group), two MDMA sessions about a month apart within a psychotherapy programme of about eleven sessions were followed, about 8 weeks after the second session, by a fall in clinician-rated depression (MADRS, scale 0 to 60: from 29.6 to 10.3, as corrected in a corrigendum; change −19.3, 95% CI −14.9 to −23.7), with 9 of 12 meeting both response and remission thresholds; functional impairment also fell. There were no serious adverse events, but worsening suicidal ideation was recorded as an adverse event in 4 to 6 of the 12 (the paper gives both figures) and 2 received benzodiazepines and zopiclone after dosing. The raters were not blind, almost all participants were self-referred, entry required a high score, and there was no control group, so the fall cannot be attributed to MDMA; the 7-month follow-up was not read. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small study in Norway, 12 adults with depression had two MDMA sessions with talking therapy. About two months later, depression scores had dropped a lot, and 9 of the 12 were much better. But there was no group without MDMA, and the people rating depression knew everyone had taken it.
population: Adults with DSM-5 major depressive disorder (single or recurrent, without psychotic features; current episode 12 weeks to 2 years) and a MADRS of 20 or more; excluded: psychotic disorders, mania, personality disorders, eating disorders with purging, substance use disorders, serious suicide risk and cardiovascular risk; psychotropic medicines tapered
exposure: MDMA in two open-label day-long sessions about 4 weeks apart within MDMA-assisted therapy (three preparatory and six integration sessions)
outcome: Change in MADRS from baseline to about 8 weeks after the second session (primary); Sheehan Disability Scale; response and remission; adverse events
magnitude: MADRS 29.6 (SD 4.9) at baseline and 10.3 (8.3) at the outcome visit (corrigendum; first printed as 9.7, SD 10.0); change −19.3 (SD 8.3), bootstrap 95% CI −14.9 to −23.7, P < 0.001; responders (fall of 50% or more) 9 of 12 and remitters (MADRS 12 or less) 9 of 12; SDS 21.3 to 9.7, change −11.7 (95% CI −7.6 to −15.8). Adverse events: 46 in 10 of 12 participants (15 moderate, 31 mild), none serious; worsening intensity of suicidal ideation in 6 participants (12 events) by the Results, suicidal ideation in 33.3% by the Discussion; benzodiazepines and zopiclone for 2 participants within 2 days after dosing.

evidence.locator: Results › Primary outcome, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (MADRS row)
evidence.extracted: MADRS 29.6 (4.9) at baseline; mean change −19.3 (SD 8.3) to the outcome visit about 2 months after the second MDMA session; bootstrap 95% CI −14.9 to −23.7; z = −3.06, P < 0.001; among the 9 without comorbid PTSD, change −18.1 (8.8).

evidence.locator: Corrigendum text, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; corrected Table 2 (MADRS row)
evidence.extracted: One participant's post-treatment MADRS was wrong; corrected outcome mean 10.3 (SD 8.3) instead of 9.7 (10.0); change −19.3 (−14.9 to −23.7) unchanged; responder and remitter counts unaffected.

evidence.locator: Results › Exploratory analysis, 1st paragraph; Results › Secondary outcome, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Responders (MADRS fall of 50% or more) 9 of 12 and remitters (MADRS 12 or less) 9 of 12; SDS 21.3 (6.1) to 9.7 (9.2), change −11.7 (SD 7.6), 95% CI −7.6 to −15.8, P = 0.001.

46 adverse events in 10 of 12 participants (15 moderate, 31 mild), none serious, no discontinuations; most common headache, increased suicidal ideation and jaw muscle tightness; 2 participants received benzodiazepines and zopiclone within 2 days after dosing; no serious suicidal ideation or behaviour, but 6 participants (12 events) had a worsening in the intensity of suicidal ideation.

The authors give suicidal ideation as 33.3% when comparing with MAPP1; they state that without a control group the response cannot be attributed to the treatment rather than expectancy or natural fluctuation, that MADRS raters were neither completely independent nor blinded, and that adverse events reported to the therapy team may have been under-reported.

evidence.locator: Fig. 1 (CONSORT diagram, image); Results › Feasibility, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: 15 enrolled, 3 stopped before dosing, 12 dosed and analysed with none lost afterwards; 11 of 12 self-referred and 1 referred by a study therapist.

evidence.locator: EU Clinical Trials Register, trial 2021-000805-26 (NO) › E.2 Objectives; E.5 End points; record dates
evidence.extracted: Record first entered 4 August 2021, before recruitment (January 2023); open-label phase 2 feasibility study; main objective the mean change in MADRS (10 items, each rated 0 to 6) from baseline to about 12 weeks; registered secondary endpoint a subjective-effects scale, which the article does not report.

risk_of_bias.note: Critical: no comparison; unblinded raters; regression to the mean.

grade.reasoning: One single-arm open-label study of 12 people: non-randomized, starts low. Risk of bias two levels (ROBINS-I critical): no comparison group; about eleven psychotherapy sessions, themselves an effective treatment for depression; entry required a MADRS of 20 or more, inviting regression to the mean; self-referred participants with probably high expectations; raters not blind. Imprecision one level: 12 participants. Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to this population and endpoint. The relation is 'insufficient evidence': the design cannot show whether MDMA changes depression, and the statement describes what was observed.

statement: In adults with severe PTSD and no current alcohol use disorder (the first phase 3 trial, MAPP1; 82 of 90 with data), MDMA-assisted therapy compared with placebo plus the same therapy was followed by small changes in self-reported hazardous drinking (AUDIT, scale 0 to 40: −1.0 vs +0.4 points; P = 0.04 without adjustment, P = 0.52 after adjusting for the MDMA group's higher baseline) and drug use (DUDIT, scale 0 to 44: −1.4 vs −0.8; P = 0.55) by the end of the study. The questionnaires asked about the past 12 months at baseline but only about the time since treatment ended at the end, the outcomes were exploratory and self-reported in a trial where most participants probably knew their allocation, and people with current substance use disorders other than mild alcohol or cannabis use disorder were excluded. The evidence is insufficient to say whether MDMA-assisted therapy changes alcohol or drug use in people with PTSD; drug-use scores did not rise in either group. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one PTSD trial of 90 people, those who had MDMA therapy did not clearly change their drinking or drug use compared with those who had a dummy pill. But almost no one had a drinking or drug problem to begin with, and people reported their own use.
population: Adults with severe PTSD (CAPS-5 of 35 or more) in MAPP1; current mild alcohol or cannabis use disorder (or moderate in early remission) allowed and other substance use disorders within 12 months excluded; in the analysed set none had a current alcohol use disorder
exposure: MDMA in three sessions within manualized therapy
comparator: Inactive placebo with the same therapy
outcome: Change in AUDIT and DUDIT scores from baseline to study termination
magnitude: AUDIT change −1.02 (SD 3.52; n = 42) vs +0.40 (2.70; n = 40), unadjusted P = 0.0436, Hedges' g 0.45; adjusted for baseline AUDIT, P = 0.52. DUDIT change −1.36 (3.00) vs −0.78 (5.39), P = 0.5452, g 0.13. Baseline AUDIT 4.26 vs 2.83 (Table 1; P = .10).

evidence.extracted: AUDIT change −1.02 (3.52) on MDMA vs +0.40 (2.70) on placebo, P = 0.0436, Hedges' g = .45; no longer significant after adjusting for baseline AUDIT (P = 0.52); baseline difference P = .10.

risk_of_bias.note: Exploratory self-report; changed recall window; analysis-dependent result.

grade.reasoning: From a randomized trial: starts high. Risk of bias two levels (RoB 2 high for measurement and for selection of the reported result): exploratory self-reported questionnaires, a recall window that changed between the two measurements, probable unblinding, complete-case data, and a result that depends on whether the baseline imbalance is adjusted for. Imprecision one level: small differences on long scales and a wide range of plausible effects for drug use. Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to people with PTSD without current substance use disorders. The relation is 'insufficient evidence' because neither a change nor its absence is shown with precision.

statement: In the small trials of MDMA-assisted therapy outside PTSD read for this page (anxiety with a life-threatening illness, 13 on MDMA and 5 on placebo; social anxiety in autistic adults, 8 and 4; major depression, 12 open-label; couples, 6 and 8 couples open-label), no serious adverse event was attributed to MDMA and no participant stopped treatment because of side effects. During sessions MDMA was followed more often than placebo by jaw clenching (11 of 13 vs 1 of 5), thirst (11 of 13 vs 2 of 5), sweating (9 of 13 vs 0 of 5) and headache (8 of 13 vs 1 of 5), and in autistic adults by anxiety (6 of 8 vs 1 of 4); in the following week by fatigue and needing more sleep (12 of 13 each vs 3 and 2 of 5); blood pressure, pulse and temperature rose during sessions without needing treatment. Suicidal ideation was recorded as an adverse event in 2 of 8 autistic adults on MDMA (and 1 of 4 on placebo), and worsening suicidal ideation in 4 to 6 of 12 people with depression; 2 of those 12 received benzodiazepines and zopiclone for anxiety and insomnia after dosing. Side effects were mostly collected as spontaneous reports or by the treating therapists, and with at most 13 people on MDMA per trial, rare or delayed harms could not be detected. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In small trials of MDMA therapy for problems other than PTSD, no one had a serious side effect from MDMA. Short-lived effects such as a tight jaw, thirst, sweating, headache and tiredness were common. These trials were too small to show rare harms.
population: Adults in published trials of MDMA-assisted therapy outside PTSD that were read in full: anxiety with a life-threatening illness, social anxiety in autistic adults, major depressive disorder, and couples in which one partner had PTSD
exposure: MDMA in two (occasionally three) supervised sessions within psychotherapy
comparator: Inactive placebo with the same psychotherapy in two trials; none in the open-label studies
outcome: Adverse events, expected reactions, vital signs and suicidal ideation during and after MDMA sessions
magnitude: Anxiety with a life-threatening illness (MDMA 13, placebo 5): during sessions jaw clenching 11 vs 1, thirst 11 vs 2, dry mouth 9 vs 1, perspiration 9 vs 0, headache 8 vs 1; in the next 7 days fatigue 12 vs 3, needing more sleep 12 vs 2, insomnia 9 vs 2; peak temperature 37.3 vs 36.9 °C. Autistic adults (8, 4): anxiety 6 vs 1, difficulty concentrating 5 vs 1; suicidal ideation 2 vs 1; peak systolic pressure, pulse and temperature higher on MDMA (maximum pulse 114, maximum temperature 37.7 °C). Depression (12, open-label): 46 adverse events in 10 participants, none serious; worsening suicidal ideation in 4 to 6. Veteran couples (8 dosed): headache 6 of 8 within 7 days, raised blood pressure 3 of 8. Serious adverse events attributed to MDMA: none among the 58 people given MDMA in these five studies (counting the 5 placebo participants of the life-threatening-illness trial who later took MDMA open-label).

evidence.extracted: During the two blinded sessions, MDMA (13) vs placebo (5): jaw clenching 11 vs 1, thirst 11 vs 2, dry mouth 9 vs 1, perspiration 9 vs 0, headache 8 vs 1; in the following 7 days fatigue 12 vs 3, needing more sleep 12 vs 2, insomnia 9 vs 2; reactions decreased over the week.

Treatment-emergent adverse events infrequent and nearly equal between groups; serious events only from cancer recurrence or progression (one death about a year after stopping, unrelated to MDMA); only peak temperature differed (37.3 vs 36.9 °C); no serious suicidal ideation or behaviour; no discontinuation because of adverse effects related to MDMA.

evidence.locator: Results › Safety, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Tables 4 and 5
evidence.extracted: No serious adverse events; during sessions anxiety in 6 of 8 on MDMA vs 1 of 4 on placebo and difficulty concentrating 5 vs 1; one severe headache on MDMA; suicidal ideation as an adverse event in 2 of 8 vs 1 of 4, pre-existing in medical history; depressed mood 2 of 8 vs 0.

Mean peak systolic blood pressure (P = 0.021), pulse (P = 0.015) and temperature (P < 0.001) higher on MDMA; maximum pulse 114 bpm, maximum temperature 37.7 °C; no systolic pressure above 180 or diastolic above 110 mmHg; values back to pre-drug levels by session end.

46 adverse events in 10 of 12, 15 moderate and 31 mild, none serious, no discontinuations; most common headache, increased suicidal ideation and jaw muscle tightness; benzodiazepines and zopiclone for 2 participants after dosing; worsening intensity of suicidal ideation in 6 participants (12 events).
Suicidal ideation given as 33.3% in the comparison with MAPP1; adverse events were reported to the therapy team, which may have led to under-reporting.

No serious adverse events; every veteran had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event; headache 75.0%, feeling warm 37.5%, increased blood pressure 37.5%, nausea, decreased appetite and sadness 25.0% each within 7 days of an MDMA session; no high suicide risk on the C-SSRS.
All six couples completed the protocol; no serious adverse events; the most common reactions after MDMA sessions were diminished appetite, anxiety, headache and jaw tightness.

risk_of_bias.note: Spontaneous or therapist-recorded side effects; possible under-reporting.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim about what was recorded in these trials: starts low. Risk of bias one level: side effects were collected as spontaneous reports or by the treating therapists, which the depression trial's authors say may have led to under-reporting, and the counts of suicidal ideation differ within one paper; this could materially change the figures. Imprecision is not rated down separately because the claim gives counts and states that rare or delayed harms could not be detected. Status 'replicated': the same pattern of short-lived sympathomimetic and mood reactions, without serious adverse events attributed to MDMA, was recorded by independent teams in the United States and Norway. To be joined with the other reader's claim from the cross-indication reviews.
